en: Whenever it vanished, Manas’s
Thoughts were torn apart.
That Almambet, entrusted for safekeeping,
Whom he had loaded up—
Upon the horse beneath him then,
Had he not loaded him?
Shining as though moonlight fell upon it,
Sarala the swift steed appeared.
Sarala with the cow-like rump,
With a mottled blue cloud wrapped about it from the sky,
Had carried Almambet’s body
From the shouting multitude of troops
And escaped with it unharmed.
It had no tongue to tell its story,
That blessed creature, wiser than other beasts.
Without swallowing even a sip of water,
Without crunching a blade of grass,
Without stopping to rest by day,
Without reckoning the time of day,
Sarala, once like shining moonlight,
Came leaning forward, blackened all over.
That apple-like golden head
Was covered in dark blood.
Its ravenous mouth gaped open;
Foam scattered from its mouth.
Then it lowered its head to the earth.
Though Sarala was a beast,
One could adore that swift steed.
The creature had taken up mourning.
Facing toward broad Talas,
The creature had stretched out in flight.
Having lost its mane and tail,
The creature had gained the name Short-Tail.
Sarala, once so radiant,
This year had become Sarala Short-Tail.
Each time it bent down, its lips were sore.
Not a fingernail-sized patch was sound.
The place for the sweat-pad was raw;
All the flesh of its back was raw;
The place for the saddle was raw;
Its back was raw in many places.
Then cow-rumped Sarala,
Though it was only a beast,
Had endured much trouble.
Traveling on a distant journey,
Sarala had grown thin.
Carrying your dear Alma,
It had lost all its bodily strength
And become a miserable creature.
Having lost its mane and tail,
It had gained the name Short-Tail.
At that time Sarala
Had acquired a sorry name.
Upon the sloping ridge of It-Olbos,
Sarala had trotted onward.
Humiliation no beast had seen—
O warrior, Sarala had seen it.
Almambet’s body
Sarala had carried as a load.
Suffering no beast could bear—
Then Sarala had borne it.
Many a saddle-shaped mountain pass
Sarala had crossed.
Many a pass and stony road
Sarala had traveled.
Taking the direct path steadily,
Sarala had trotted onward.
The fair face of Lord Manas
Sarala had then beheld.
Almambet’s body,
Having brought it safe and sound,
Into the hands of Lord Bakai
Sarala had then delivered.
Almambet’s body
The precious lion carried with him.
The four corners of the round world—
The precious warrior searched them as he went.
When he came to At-Bashy,
He cut a way toward Chech-Tobo, they say.
Azizkan’s only son
He laid to rest at Chech-Tobo, they say.
Cleansed of the dark faith,
He had fled the unbelievers and become a stranger.
The yellow willow he had planted—
His willow remained in Beijing.
Fashioned from pure gold,
His throne remained in Beijing.
He scattered what he had gathered,
Seeking only the faith.
“Rather than reign over unbelievers,
I shall go and settle in Mecca.
Rather than be khan of unbelievers,
I shall become an ordinary Burut.”
Then he repudiated his idols
And abandoned his Chinese people.
For the sake of the other world,
Because that tormenting hell existed,
He stained his golden throne with blood.
“He will not enter the Muslim faith,” he said,
“He knows nothing of what is lawful,” he said.
He stained his golden throne with blood
And laid low his father Azizkan.
When greatly provoked to anger,
He made his silver throne bloody.
“Though I tell him every day, he will not listen,” he said,
And laid low Kün Jangjung.
Cleansed of the dark faith,
When your Alma escaped,
They fought, barely surviving,
Until the pliant reeds had ripened,
Until the autumn gossamer fell,
Battling fiercely for six whole months.
To Beijing, untouched by Solomon,
He had returned as a sultan.
For the utterly pure, sovereign faith,
He was parted from his mother Altynai.
Your Alma took up a spear and broke the old faith.
When, against imperial Beijing,
He went upon campaign,
Your Alma died, struck down by a bullet.
For the martyr slain by unbelievers,
They now slaughtered his Sarala
And laid your Alma to rest at Chech-Tobo.
“An unbeliever’s bullet struck him down,” they said.
Through this, Chech-Tobo
Now became a great sacred shrine.
When they slaughtered Sarala,
When they laid your Alma to rest,
It was as though Almambet had just died,
As though the suffering had just begun.
His friend Manas the leopard,
Weeping and lamenting without cease,
Came to Almambet’s court,
Roaring out his grief.
Stunned and losing his senses,
Manas was no longer well.
“You who girded a leather belt about your waist,
When seven tumen of troops came,
Attacked with your coat draped over your shoulders;
Golden crest, tasselled sash,
Only son of Azizkan—
My friend Almambet, take me with you!
The currants in the ravine—
That we may go hand in hand,
Alas for this day, my Alma, take me with you!
My Alma, a black-cheeked white axe—
Who will fit its haft without making it crooked?
To Beijing sunk in a dark night,
Who will lead along the familiar road?
My banner of red steel,
Almambet, my gift come from China!
When a daughter-damned day of trouble falls upon me,
The one I need in hardship,
My support when I climb upward—
How can I stand without dying?
Alas for this day, my Alma, my prop!
From my firmly secured fortress,
Am I truly to be parted?
From my champion Alma, my lion,
Azizkan’s only son,
My dear Alma, who trotted upon Sarala!
We were not born of the same father.
Allah Most High, the one God,
Drove my champion from China.
Don't throw stones,
Almambet the lion, the noble lion!
Now that my dear Alma has died,
Can I stand looking on alive?
My noble Alma, my lion—
Can I surrender him to the black earth?
My day is gone, Khan Bakai.
The powder in my powder-flask has spilled.
Grief-stricken Manas, the precious lion,
Today lost hope of that stout khan.
My resource is gone, Khan Bakai.
See how my honor has been upheld!
I am grateful to Allah:
Today my dear Alma’s body has been found.
Roaring month after month,
Like a wind-swept land amid the crags,
Whoever came, never drawing back,
Like my black-eared lion,
My support in spear combat,
Almambet, my prop!”
Mourning and weeping bitterly,
At Almambet’s court,
Weeping, “My precious Alma!”
Then Manas wailed and doubled over.
Yellow poison mixed with brain matter
Khan Manas vomited up
And fell straight down upon his head.
Then your leopard-mother Kanykei
Burst into piercing cries.
Supporting the warrior’s head, sobbing,
“My sultan, yellow poison mixed with brain matter—
This is an illness that brings dire distress.
Warrior, did you have a wound at your nape?”
“My lady, let me tell you of the wound in my back.
In the marshland of broad Beijing,
While I was performing my prayers,
When I laid my head down in prostration,
Ajybai, son of Khan Argyn,
Was sleeping far away.
With cotton sash and ample boots,
Kongurbay, khan of the monks,
Stretched out and thrust his spear into me.
When the spear’s point jutted out
And remained within my back,
Ajybai, son of Khan Argyn—
I told him to pull firmly; he pulled loosely
And twisted the spear.
The steel point snapped
And broke off within my back.
By the time I reached this place,
The opening had closed,
But deep inside it had festered.
Look closely, tend it and take pains:
This is the wound within my back.”
Kanykei, the leopard-woman,
Burst into bitter tears,
Then wailed with a piercing cry:
“Alas, my lord—may ruin strike!
I failed to see the wound within your back.
Your hour of death has come;
My means of saving you are gone.
In that battle at broad Beijing,
In the marshland of Kara-Kol,
While you were performing your prayers,
Had I been a man instead of a woman,
Before my Blood-Shedder,
Had I been his sentry,
When the fierce one stabbed my Blood-Shedder,
Had I been the companion Ajybai,
Would I not have speared the uncircumcised one?
Would I not have tested the swift horse?
Would I not have brought upon Beijing
Havoc no human had wrought?
Would I not have beaten him till he sprawled,
That uncircumcised one, Kongurbay?
Would I not have made Beijing suffer
Havoc no human had wrought?
Would I not have had the butcher slaughtered?
Would I not have brought a campaign upon Beijing?
Would I not have broken the pole?
Had I been a man instead of a female,
Would I not have shown the fierce one what I could do?
Would I not have brought upon Beijing
Devastation no mortal had wrought?
(The Blood-Shedder’s hour of death had come;
The unfortunate woman’s means were gone.)
When the champion came from Beijing,
When his hapless wife saw him safe,
When we lay upon the narrow bed,
When we were immersed in pleasure,
When I laid my arm across him,
When I drew him close against my breast,
